newsitem.title: USA: Odds said likely Fed to tighten at March 25 FOMC.
newsitem.headline: Odds said likely Fed to tighten at March 25 FOMC.

text.p: The Federal Reserve, concerned about safeguarding the conditions that would allow the U.S. expansion to sail into its seventh year, is likely to tighten credit when its convenes on March 25, according to a source close to the central bank and some Fed watchers.

"Before Congress, (Fed Chairman Alan) Greenspan repeated his December message and more," the source told Reuters. "This is twice now that he has been linking asset prices to monetary policy. He certainly reminded everyone that the imbalances in the economy are in the stock market."

Greenspan, in his two-part Humphrey-Hawkins testimony delivered to Congress last week and again on Wednesday, sounded words of caution about "excessive optimism" in financial asset markets. On December 5, 1996, the Chairman had already expressed concern over "irrational exuberance."
That remark came two days after Greenspan presided over a seminar at the Fed Board on the topic of the stock market and how to interpret it.
A number of academics specializing in stocks and monetary policy, as well as senior Wall Street stock gurus presented their views at the seminar and spoke to Greenspan.

"Greenspan is worried about the eventual market fall. He's been worried about it for some time. Now, he's worrying out loud," the source added, noting that such concern has existed at the Fed since last summer. "What the Fed is doing is (in order) to sustain long-term non-inflationary growth."
The source further said it was likely the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) would inch up the 5.25-percent federal funds rate when it meets on March 25.
"The reason will be, I think, similar to 1994, a preemptive strike before it gets started," the source said. "Definitely, Greenspan has warned the markets."
Greenspan made clear the Fed does not -- and cannot -- decide at what level financial assets should be priced.
But he warned that when earnings expectations built into asset prices are not met, "the unwinding of these financial excesses can act to amplify a downturn in economic activity."
The source said, "That is the concern" for the Fed during a long-toothed expansion where financial markets have priced in as much future good economic news as possible.
The source also pointed out that a preemptive action would be limited in scope since the inflation-adjusted real funds rate now is much higher than in 1994 when it was zero.
John Campbell, professor of economics at Harvard University, is among the experts who have studied the relationship between market performance and the economy.

"When prices get high relative to earnings and dividends, there is a a tendency for the rate of return to be lower over the subsequent years," Campbell said. "That does not necessarily lead to crashes. But even if the prices stay were they are, the rate of return will be very low."
Several Fed watchers, such as former Fed Board staff director Stephen Axilrod, agreed the healthy expansion allows the Fed to take out insurance against potential imbalances.
"Greenspan has given a warning we're on the verge of a tightening," Axilrod, now an adviser at MFR Inc, also said.
"The one imbalance that concerns Greenspan is the stock market, because, if you go too far ahead, you could have a sharp drop which could affect the economy," Axilrod added.
"Before, the Fed did not have enough confidence to tighten in the face of the real side of the economy. The economy is now showing enough strength to take that step," he stated.
Nomura Securities International chief economist David Resler said Greenspan's concern indicated he does not share the upbeat economic outlook that the markets have.

"Greenspan hinted he does not believe the moderate growth that the FOMC anticipates, combined with tight labor markets, can allow for the growth in earnings that is built into current asset values," Resler said.
Joseph Carson, fixed-income chief economist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell, said, "Greenspan is more worried about the process of asset inflation leading to price inflation."

Carson said Greenspan even signaled that "the size of the move this time will be much smaller" as he "compared 1994 and 1997 and said the scale will be much smaller" than the 1994 tightening cycle that doubled the funds rate in just a year.
"Greenspan was as plain as in 1994, clearly alerting the market he was going to raise rates," Carson added.

Ken Bercuson, head of research at SBC Warburg, noted Greenspan has made a clear-cut case about the need for preemptive monetary policy, before imbalances have actually developed and are costly to correct.

"He said that it's specifically because the Fed tightened in 1994 that inflation did not rise," Bercuson noted. "He emphasized the Fed's task is to prevent imbalances from forming, because correcting these imbalances, once they exist, is far more costly to the overall economy," Bercuson said.
